analysis.one_liner: Blocks emergency oil reserve releases until the Interior Department plans more federal-land oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced with 0 cosponsors, it sat in two House committees until the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop the Energy Department from selling, exchanging, or loaning oil out of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve — the emergency stockpile the government uses to temper fuel price spikes — until the Interior Department issues or updates a plan to increase oil and gas production on federal land, including offshore waters. The only exceptions are a severe energy supply interruption or a release Congress itself orders. National parks, wildlife refuges, wilderness areas, marine sanctuaries, and tribal lands are excluded from the drilling-plan requirement.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies. The bill would use every future reserve release as leverage: before the government could tap the emergency stockpile to bring pump prices down, Interior would have to commit to production increases on top of lease sales it had already scheduled, including in offshore waters. That converts a consumer price-relief tool into a bargaining chip for expanded industry access to federal land.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would require the Interior Secretary to issue or update a plan to increase oil and gas production on federal land before any drawdown of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, with each plan including actions on top of lease sales already scheduled under the Mineral Leasing Act and the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act.

It would define 'federal land' to include Outer Continental Shelf waters, extending the production mandate offshore, while carving out only parks, refuges, wilderness areas, marine sanctuaries, and tribal lands.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and taxpayers. The reserve is a public emergency asset paid for by taxpayers; this bill would encumber it so that relief at the pump could be withheld until a new federal drilling plan was issued — precisely during price spikes. If emergency releases were delayed or blocked, drivers and businesses burning fuel would bear the cost in higher prices.

drawbacks.text: The plan precondition could delay or block emergency reserve releases during price spikes — the exact situations the reserve exists for — since no release would be allowed until Interior issued a new production plan, which has no deadline.

Supporters' own rationale was that drawing down the reserve without boosting production runs down the stockpile without addressing supply; the bill's answer is to condition a short-term price-relief tool on a longer-term leasing plan, which does not necessarily produce oil quickly or cheaply for consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to oil and gas companies, which would gain a guaranteed push for expanded federal drilling — including offshore — triggered by every reserve release. The costs fall on consumers, who would see an emergency price-relief tool held hostage to a new drilling plan, and on the reserve itself as a flexible public asset. The protected-land exclusions are a real safeguard, but they do not change the basic trade: consumer emergency relief traded for industry leverage.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to two House committees, got no cosponsors, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2023 without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven Palazzo introduced the Strategic Production Response Act on December 8, 2021, with no cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Natural Resources Committee, and on December 17, 2021 to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee.
No further action was ever taken; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve stayed unconditionally available for releases — and it was used to temper prices during 2022. Oil and gas companies gained no new lever tying reserve use to expanded federal drilling; consumers kept the emergency stockpile without strings.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers; the oil reserve stayed unconditionally available

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the sole sponsor was a Republican with zero cosponsors, and the Democratic-controlled committees never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would make expanded federal drilling — beyond lease sales already scheduled, including offshore waters — a precondition for any emergency reserve release. That uses consumer pain at the pump as leverage for more industry access to federal land, while reserve releases that lower prices would be delayed or blocked.
